speaker: Elena Verna
title: 10 growth tactics that never work | Elena Verna (Amplitude, Miro, Dropbox, SurveyMonkey)
question: In a mature SaaS company with slowing growth, why does hiring a head of growth or building a growth team usually fail to reverse the decline?
guest: When a mature company's growth slows down, they hire a shiny head of growth to fix the problem, thinking they'll bring this person in and growth will accelerate. That just does not happen. If the overall business is slowing down, your head of growth is destined to fail because the reason business is slowing down is much deeper than not having a growth team. A growth team can optimize and maybe lift it by 10 to 15 percent, which is on the upper end if there is a slowdown trajectory. If you have core product and core marketing issues, a growth team will not be able to fix them for you. Growth can amplify great product-market fit and help you grow faster once you're already growing, but if your product-market fit is degrading or being eaten by a competitor, growth is helpless. At that company size you need fairly large growth teams across every product flow, so it's a huge expense that might barely return one-to-one ROI rather than a J-curve. If you're declining, see at least that core product and marketing can plateau and stop the decline first before putting growth on it.

points.core: Growth teams amplify existing product-market fit instead of fixing core product erosion.
points.note: Accept: growth teams optimize working PMF and cannot repair degrading PMF, core product weaknesses, competitive displacement, or broken market strategy. Do not credit: generic hiring platitudes or claiming a great growth leader can turn around a core product decline.

points.core: Growth optimizations yield modest lifts that cannot reverse a structural business slowdown.
points.note: Accept: optimization lifts are small (e.g., ~10-15% at best) and covering mature product surfaces requires expensive teams that barely break even rather than creating a J-curve turnaround. Do not credit: vague claims that growth is hard without the modest-lift/ROI constraint.

points.core: Core teams must halt the decline before growth investments generate turnaround returns.
points.note: Accept: core product and marketing teams need to plateau or stabilize the declining trajectory first before layering on growth to accelerate recovery. Do not credit: generic advice to align cross-functional teams without sequencing stabilization before growth.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Because slowing growth in a mature SaaS company is usually a structural problem, not an optimization problem, and a growth team is an optimization tool.

Growth teams work by tuning funnels: acquisition channels, onboarding, activation, pricing pages, conversion and retention loops. That produces real gains when a product with strong market fit has untapped demand. In a mature company, the decline typically comes from things those levers can't touch: the core market is saturated, the best channels are exhausted and customer acquisition costs are rising, competitors have commoditized the product, or churn reflects a value gap rather than onboarding friction. Experiments then yield small, incremental lifts on a flattening curve.

The role is also usually set up to fail organizationally. The head of growth is handed a revenue target without authority over product roadmap, pricing, sales or the budget. The hire becomes a way for leadership to delegate a strategic question they haven't answered themselves.

Reversing the decline generally requires a new S-curve: new products, segments, geographies, or a repositioning. Those are CEO-level bets, with growth teams amplifying them afterward rather than substituting for them.

points.why: The response explains why growth levers amplify strong product-market fit and cannot repair competitive erosion or a gap in core product value.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Hiring a head of growth or building a growth team usually fails to reverse a mature SaaS slowdown because growth teams amplify existing value rather than create new demand. Mature companies typically stall for structural reasons: core market saturation, exhausted acquisition channels, competitive commoditization, or eroding product-market fit. Escaping that plateau requires executive-level bets—such as launching second-act products, entering new customer segments, or overhauling pricing and business models—not incremental funnel tweaks.

Growth teams are built to remove friction across activation, self-serve conversion, and expansion loops, which yields diminishing marginal gains once core workflows are already reasonably tuned and market ceilings bind. Worse, growth leaders rarely control core R&D, brand positioning, or enterprise sales motions, leaving them trapped in organizational turf wars without the levers needed to reignite durable revenue. Pressured for quick wins, they often resort to short-term tactics like aggressive upsells, paywalls, or discounting that inflate local metrics while eroding customer trust and accelerating churn. Ultimately, delegating a company-wide strategic inflection to an optimization team mistakes a product and market ceiling for a funnel problem.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Hiring a head of growth usually fails because it treats a strategic problem as an execution problem. In a mature SaaS company, growth typically slows for structural reasons. The core market is saturated, the product has become commoditized or been overtaken, the pricing and packaging no longer fit how customers buy, or the original acquisition channels have stopped working. The S-curve of the original product is flattening.

Growth teams are good at optimizing an existing curve: onboarding, activation, conversion, and expansion experiments. Those wins are real but incremental, and they come from a shrinking pool of opportunity. A growth team can't create a new S-curve. That takes new products, new customer segments, new markets, or a different business model, and those decisions belong to the CEO, product leadership and the board.

A growth team also usually lacks authority over the levers that matter, like the roadmap, pricing and sales motion. As a bolt-on function, it often clashes with product and marketing. Leadership gets to feel it has acted while avoiding the harder work of rethinking product-market, channel and model fit.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
In a mature SaaS company, slowing growth is usually a structural problem rather than an optimization problem. Growth teams excel at reducing friction, refining onboarding, and extracting more efficiency from working acquisition loops. However, when a mature business decelerates, the root cause is typically market saturation, a flattening core S-curve, intensifying competition, or eroding product-market fit. Incremental funnel tweaks and A/B tests cannot overcome a tapped-out market; reversing structural decline requires a new growth engine, such as a new product line, customer segment, or distribution model.

Even when a growth team identifies high-leverage opportunities, mature organizations rarely give them the authority to execute. Core product teams fiercely guard the roadmap, sales teams resist self-serve or pricing changes that threaten commissions, and leadership often expects quick wins rather than multi-quarter strategic shifts. Isolated from the core product and go-to-market motions, the head of growth gets relegated to superficial optimizations that cannot move the needle at scale.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
A growth team can improve conversion, onboarding, and retention, but those gains are usually too small to offset the forces slowing a mature SaaS business. As the customer base gets larger, the company needs more new revenue just to sustain the same percentage growth. Meanwhile, its best acquisition channels may be saturated, its core market may have fewer untapped buyers, and churn can eat into new sales.

Hiring a head of growth also tends to put one team in charge of a number that depends on decisions across the company. If the slowdown calls for a new customer segment, a stronger product, different pricing, or a new sales motion, the growth team needs the authority and resources to make those changes. Without them, it can run successful experiments and still leave the growth trajectory largely unchanged.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A new head of growth can improve how customers find, adopt, and pay for a product. But in a mature SaaS company, growth often slows because the easiest-to-reach customers have already bought, existing customers have little room to expand, or the product no longer gives enough customers a reason to stay. A larger revenue base also means the company must add more revenue each year just to maintain the same growth rate.

A growth team usually controls only some of those levers. Better campaigns and onboarding can lift conversion, but they have limited impact if the next customer segment needs a different product or if churn erases the gains. Hiring a leader gives someone responsibility for the growth target. Reversing the slowdown depends on identifying what is holding growth back and giving the people who control product, pricing, sales, or retention the authority and resources to change it.
